headline: Sentence Scramble: Build Correct Sentences Together
problemStatement: Students may know individual vocabulary items yet struggle to arrange them into a grammatical sentence. Sentence Scramble makes word order visible: learners tap the available tiles into a sentence, check their attempt, and can try again before the class reviews the correct structure.
outcomes: Notice word order and sentence patterns while actively rebuilding a sentence.
Practice reading for meaning instead of guessing from isolated vocabulary.
Learn from common wrong orders and compare them with the correct sentence.
howItWorks: The game generates a short sentence at the chosen difficulty and mixes its words into tiles.
Students arrange the words on their phones. Repeated words remain separate tiles, so a sentence with two instances of the same word can still be solved.
In race mode, correct answers earn points by speed, and a wrong order can be corrected without losing the chance to participate.
The teacher can reveal the first word as a hint. At the end, the tiles form the answer and the most common wrong order can be discussed anonymously.
teacherUseCases: Use easy sentences for a quick grammar warm-up, or raise the difficulty when students are ready to handle longer structures.
After a round, ask students to explain a common slip and say the corrected sentence aloud.

faq.q: Can students try again after a wrong order?
faq.a: Yes. In race mode, a wrong submission receives feedback and the learner can submit another arrangement. Correct solvers are tracked separately.

faq.q: What happens when a sentence repeats a word?
faq.a: The game keeps repeated words as distinct tiles instead of removing duplicates. This lets students place both copies in the sentence.

faq.q: Does the teacher have to reveal the whole answer?
faq.a: No. The teacher can offer a first-word hint, keep the round going, and reveal the full sentence when it is time for class review.

faq.q: Can the class learn from incorrect attempts?
faq.a: The game tracks wrong orders and can show the common slip anonymously. Use it to discuss why that order sounds less natural and how the grammar works.
